p: After concluding the Treaty of Tilsit with Napoleon in 1807, Emperor Alexander I of Russia wrote on 24 September 1807 to King Gustav IV Adolf of Sweden that peace between them depended on Sweden accepting the treaty's limits, which in practice meant cutting off trade with Britain. The king, who viewed Napoleon as the Antichrist, secured an alliance with Britain on 8 February 1808. In Saint Petersburg his stubbornness was seen as a convenient pretext for occupying Finland. Swedish plans assumed that war in winter was impossible, while Russian planners chose a winter offensive, when frozen seas would isolate Finland.

On 21 February 1808, 24,000 Russian troops under Friedrich Wilhelm von Buxhoeveden crossed the border and took Loviisa; war was not declared until April. Helsinki fell on 2 March and Turku on 21 March, as the Swedish army under General Wilhelm Mauritz Klingspor withdrew northwards. Sveaborg, with a garrison of 6,000 men and over 700 cannons, surrendered on 6 May 1808 after prolonged negotiations, its commander Admiral Carl Olof Cronstedt believing resistance futile, and the Russians gained most of the Swedish archipelago fleet intact. Swedish counter-attacks at Siikajoki and Revolax halted the offensive for a time, and Finns rose in guerrilla fighting.

Reinforced to 55,000 men against an estimated 36,000, the Russians attacked again in August, and Count Nikolay Kamensky won the most important victory at Oravais on 14 September. By November 1808 Russian forces had overrun all of Finland, and the Convention of Olkijoki of 19 November obliged the Swedish army to leave. In March 1809 Russian columns crossed the frozen Gulf of Bothnia, occupying the Åland Islands and entering Umeå on 24 March. King Gustav IV, blamed for the loss of Finland, was dethroned by a coup in Stockholm on 13 March, and his uncle became Charles XIII of Sweden.

By the Treaty of Fredrikshamn of 17 September 1809 Sweden also gave up its domains east of the Torne river. The Grand Duchy of Finland kept the Gustavian constitution of 1772 with only slight modifications until 1919, and in 1812 Russia attached to it the areas it had gained from Sweden in the 18th century, known as Old Finland. In Sweden the war was followed by a new constitution and, in 1818, by the establishment of the House of Bernadotte. Two studies of 2015 by the political scientists Jan Teorell and Bo Rothstein argue that the defeat moved Swedish elites to reform the bureaucracy.

notes: The article spells the Russian commander Buxhoeveden and Buxhoevden, and the Swedish king Gustav IV Adolf, Gustav Adolf, Gustaf IV Adolf and Gustav IV; I used Buxhoeveden and Gustav IV Adolf.
The naval actions, the British fleet's part and the many landings of 1808 were left out for length.
